author: mikeschinkel
message:
Fix mdns publishing service to stop growing json cache

- `pgrep` could not see the `avahi-publish` processes so it was constantly thinking they had not been started and thus kept adding to the cached JSON.
- Used `avahi-resolve` instead to check if a domain had been published rather than trying to get a list of published domains.
- The downside of using `avahi-resolve` isif it is not already published then it waits a timeout before it returns
- OTOH since this is a background task running on a timer the timeout will only ever create issues when modifying the script and having to wait for timeout while debugging. Hopefully this won't be needed much.
- See https://chat.openai.com/share/27c1d73c-015b-4546-b1fa-7b9f55a6b775 for background.

conversations.prompt:
I have a Bash script named `ensure-traefik-routes-in-mdns.sh` that I have added at the end of this prompt that when run on Debian 11 it works as expected. It discovers a list of `.local` domains from a Traefik server and then uses`avahi-publish` to add them to the local network.  I can verify they are there by `ps ax | grep avahi-publish`.

However, when I run as a SystemD service with `sudo systemctl start traefik-mdns.service` the script does not work as expected even though `sudo systemctl status traefik-mdns.service` reports success. Here is the output of `sudo systemctl status traefik-mdns.service`:


Here is the contents of the service file located at `/etc/systemd/system/traefik-mdns.service`:
```

 Description=mDNS Service for Traefik Routes

 ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/ensure-traefik-routes-in-mdns.sh

```

The contents of the script `ensure-traefik-routes-in-mdns.sh` are as follows:
```
#!/usr/bin/env bash

HOST_IP_ADDRESS="$(hostname -I | awk '{print$1}')"
HOST_PORT="8081"
TRAEFIK_ROUTERS_API_URL="http://${HOST_IP_ADDRESS}:${HOST_PORT}/api/http/routers"
CACHE_FILE="/etc/traefik/traefik-mdns.json"

function is_debug {
  local is_debug="$1"
  if [ "debug" == "${is_debug}" ] ; then
    echo 1
    return
  fi
  echo 0
}

DEBUG="$(is_debug "$1")"

function debug_msg {
  local msg="$1"
  if [ $DEBUG -eq 1 ] ; then
    printf "\n%s" "${msg}"
  fi
}

function publish_domain {
  local host_ip="$1"
  local domain="$2"

  /usr/bin/avahi-publish -a "${domain}" -R "${host_ip}" &
}

function read_cached_json {
  local cached_json=""

  if [ -f "${CACHE_FILE}" ] ; then
    cached_json="$(cat "${CACHE_FILE}")"
  fi

  if [ "" != "${cached_json}" ] ; then
    echo "${cached_json}"
  else
    echo '{"domains":[]}' | sudo tee "${CACHE_FILE}"
    return
  fi
}

function write_cached_json {
  local cached_json="$1"
  printf "%s" "${cached_json}" | sudo tee "${CACHE_FILE}" >/dev/null
}

function extract_cached_domains {
  local cached_json="$1"
  if [ "${cached_json}" == "" ] ; then
    cached_json="$(read_cached_json)"
  fi
  jq -r '.domains[]|.name' <<< "${cached_json}" \
    | sort \
    | tr "\n" ' '
}

# Dedups a space-separated list of domains
function dedup_domains {
  local domains="$1"
  tr ' ' "\n" <<< "${domains}" \
    | sort \
    | uniq \
    | tr "\n" ' '
}

function cache_has_domain {
  local domain="$1"
  local cached_domains="$2"
  local query

  query="$(printf '.domains[]|select(.name=="%s")' "${domain}")"
  result="$(jq -r "${query}" <<< "${cached_domains}")"
  test "" != "${result}"
}

function add_domain {
  local domain="$1"
  local cached_domains="$2"
  local query

  query="$(printf '.domains += [{"name":"%s", "last_seen": "%s"}]' "${domain}" "$(current_iso8601_datetime)")"
  jq "${query}" <<< "${cached_domains}"
}

function update_domain {
  local domain="$1"
  local cached_domains="$2"
  local query

  query="$(printf '.domains |= map(if .name == "%s" then .last_seen = "%s" else . end)' "${domain}" "$(current_iso8601_datetime)")"
  jq "${query}" <<< "${cached_domains}"
}

function current_iso8601_datetime {
  # Example: 2023-06-29T05:52:18Z where Z means UTC
  date -u +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"
}

function retrieve_routers_json {
  curl --silent "${TRAEFIK_ROUTERS_API_URL}"
}

function discover_published_domains {
  pgrep -a avahi-publish | awk '{print $4}' | tr "\n" ' '
}

function kill_published {
  pgrep avahi-publish | xargs kill -9
}

#
function extract_retrieved_domains {
  local routers_json="$1"

  jq -e '.[] | select(.rule|contains("Host(`"))|.rule' <<< "${routers_json}" \
      | tr '`' ' ' \
      | awk '{print$2}' \
      | sort \
      | uniq \
      | tr "\n" ' '
}

# Timing out domains last seen more than 24 hours ago.
function timeout_domains {
  local timeout_hours="$1"
  local cached_json="$2"
  local map
  local query
  local yesterday_seconds

  yesterday_seconds="$(( $(date +%s) - 60*60*timeout_hours ))"
  map="$(printf 'map(select((.last_seen | strptime("%s") | mktime)' "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")"
  query="$(printf '.domains |= %s > %d))' "${map}" "${yesterday_seconds}")"
  jq "${query}" <<< "${cached_json}"
}

function main() {
  local space=' '
  local updated=0
  local routers_json
  local published_domains
  local cached_json
  local cached_domains
  local retrieved_domains
  local potential_domains
  local domain

  debug_msg "Read the cache file to find any domains that were previously there."
  cached_json="$(read_cached_json)"

  debug_msg "Time out domains last seen more than 24 hours ago."
  cached_json="$(timeout_domains 24 "${cached_json}")"

  debug_msg "Extract cached domains from cached json that was read from the cache file."
  cached_domains=$(extract_cached_domains "${cached_json}")

  debug_msg "Send an HTTP GET request to retrieve the routers JSON from Traefik API."
  routers_json="$(retrieve_routers_json)"
  if [ "${routers_json}" == "" ] ; then
    printf 'Warning: Unable to reach %s' "${TRAEFIK_ROUTERS_API_URL}" >&2
  fi

  debug_msg "Extract just the .local domains retrieved in Traefik into a space-separated string."
  retrieved_domains="$(extract_retrieved_domains "${routers_json}")"

  debug_msg "Combine Traefik-defined domains an previously cached domains into potential domains."
  potential_domains="${cached_domains} ${retrieved_domains}"

  debug_msg "Deduplicate domains after combining Traefik-defined and previously cached domains."
  potential_domains="$(dedup_domains "${potential_domains}")"

  debug_msg "Use pgrep to discover the avahi-published .local domains from list of processes."
  published_domains="$(discover_published_domains)"

  debug_msg "Loop through the domains retrieved from Traefik to see if they have been published."
  for domain in $potential_domains; do
    debug_msg "Attempt to match a .local domain retrieved from Trafik to the list of domains currently published."
    debug_msg "$(printf 'Checking if %s is published_domains...' "${domain}")"
    if [[ "${space}${published_domains}${space}" =~ ${space}${domain}${space} ]] ; then
      [ $DEBUG -eq 1 ] && printf "already published"
      debug_msg "$(printf 'Updating .last_seen %s in cache file %s.' "${domain}", "${CACHE_FILE}")"
      debug_msg 'Since the domain is already published update JSON with last seen time.'
      if cache_has_domain "${domain}" "${cached_json}" ; then
        cached_json="$(update_domain "${domain}" "${cached_json}")"
      else
        cached_json="$(add_domain "${domain}" "${cached_json}")"
      fi
      debug_msg 'Now look at the next domain.'
      continue
    fi
    printf "Publishing %s\n" "${domain}"
    if ! publish_domain "${HOST_IP_ADDRESS}" "${domain}"; then
      printf 'Error: Unable to publish %s' "${domain}" >&2
    fi
    debug_msg "$(printf 'Adding %s to cache file %s.' "${domain}" "${CACHE_FILE}")"
    cached_json="$(add_domain "${domain}" "${cached_json}")"
    updated=1
    debug_msg "Write updated JSON to CACHE_FILE"
  done
  if [ "" != "${retrieved_domains}" ]; then
    debug_msg "Writing cache."
    write_cached_json "${cached_json}"
  fi
  if [ $DEBUG -eq 1 ]; then
    printf "\n"
  fi
  if [ $updated -eq 1 ]; then
    printf "\n"
  fi
}

main
```

Can you help be diagnose why the script won't work as intended as a SystemD service but will run from the terminal command line?
conversations.answer: From the information provided, it's possible that the issue might be related to the environment in which the systemd service is running. systemd services don't have the same environment variables as an interactive shell, and your script may depend on some of these variables.Here are some steps that you can take to debug and potentially resolve the issue:Verify that the necessary commands are accessible: The systemd service may not have the same PATH as your user's interactive shell. You could specify the absolute paths for all the commands in your bash script, or set the PATH in your systemd service file.Add error logging to your script: Modify your bash script to log errors to a file. This might provide more insight into what's going wrong when the script is run as a systemd service. You can add something like the following at the beginning of your script:[CODE_BLOCK_0]This will redirect all error messages to /path/to/your/logfile.log.Check environment differences: You can compare the environment variables available in the systemd service and in the interactive shell. You could modify your script to dump its environment to a file using env > /tmp/env.dump and then compare this with the environment of your interactive shell.Ensure the correct user and permissions: If your script needs to run as a specific user or requires special permissions, you should specify this in your service file using the User= and Group= directives under [Service]. Additionally, make sure the script file has the necessary executable permissions.Add Restart=on-failure in your service file: This will tell systemd to restart the service if it fails. Sometimes services fail and stop completely. This directive ensures that your service is restarted when it fails:[CODE_BLOCK_1]Try with Type=simple instead of Type=oneshot: In your systemd service file, you have specified Type=oneshot, which means that systemd considers the service started once the process exits. This can cause problems with services that spawn child processes and exit (which appears to be what your script does). You could try changing this to Type=simple.[CODE_BLOCK_2]After making these modifications, remember to reload the systemd daemon using sudo systemctl daemon-reload and then try to start your service again with sudo systemctl start traefik-mdns.service.Inspect the logs with sudo systemctl status traefik-mdns.service and journalctl -u traefik-mdns.service to see if there are any noticeable changes or errors.

conversations.prompt:
When I use `exec 2>/path/to/your/logfile.log` I get, one each apparently for the 5 domains that my script tries to publish:

```
Got SIGTERM, quitting.
Got SIGTERM, quitting.
Got SIGTERM, quitting.
Got SIGTERM, quitting.
Got SIGTERM, quitting.
```

Does this give you any further insight into the problem?
conversations.answer: Yes, the "Got SIGTERM, quitting." message indicates that the processes in your script are receiving a SIGTERM signal, which is asking them to terminate. In the context of a systemd service, it's normal for systemd to send SIGTERM to all processes in the service's control group when the service stops, which is why you're seeing those messages in your log.This issue could be arising because you're running /usr/bin/avahi-publish in the background (as indicated by the & symbol in the script). This could be problematic because when the script finishes and systemd sees that the main process has ended, it may think the service is done and send a SIGTERM signal to clean up any lingering processes. This could lead to the avahi-publish processes being killed before they have had a chance to do their work.Here's how you can handle this:Don't background the avahi-publish processes: You could try running the avahi-publish processes in the foreground. This would make the systemd service wait until all these processes have completed before it ends.Change the Type of your systemd service: If your script is expected to spawn long-running processes, you may want to consider changing the Type in your systemd service from oneshot to simple or forking, depending on the nature of your script. oneshot is suitable for scripts that do something and then exit, whereas simple and forking are more suitable for scripts that spawn long-running processes.Use RemainAfterExit option in the systemd service file: If you want systemd to consider the service as active even after the main process has exited, you can add RemainAfterExit=yes in the Service section of your systemd service file. This will keep the service in an "active" state after the main process has exited, and systemd won't send the SIGTERM signal.Here's how you might modify your systemd service file:[CODE_BLOCK_0]Remember to reload systemd configuration with systemctl daemon-reload after changing the service file.However, note that these are more like workarounds. The best solution would be to refactor your script so that it can be controlled more appropriately by systemd. It could be refactored so that it doesn't leave background processes running after the main script process exits.

conversations.prompt: What is the difference between service types `simple` and  `forking`?
conversations.answer: The Type directive in a systemd service file specifies the process behavior that systemd should expect when the service is started. The values simple and forking have different implications:Type=simple (default): With this setting, systemd expects that the process launched by ExecStart is the main process of the service. This is the default value if no Type is specified. If this process exits, systemd considers the service to be stopped.Type=forking: In this case, systemd expects that the process launched by ExecStart will fork, and that the parent process will exit when startup is complete and the service is running. The remaining child process will continue to run as the main process of the service. This is useful for services that traditionally were written to follow the Unix fork/exec model (i.e., the process "daemonizes" itself by forking a child process and then having the parent process immediately exit).For Type=forking, it's often used with the PIDFile directive, which points to the PID file of the service. This is necessary for systemd to keep track of the main (child) process.In short, use Type=simple for services that can run in the foreground and don't need to fork themselves. If your service needs to follow the traditional Unix daemon style (i.e., it needs to fork a child and have the parent process exit), use Type=forking. But as software has evolved, it's often considered better to let the process manager (in this case, systemd) handle the backgrounding of services, so Type=simple is generally preferred unless the service explicitly needs the forking behavior.

conversations.prompt:
Thank you!  The answer was for me to change the type to `forking`.  

I agree in general it is better to allow SystemD to manage this service, but I am using a service combined with a timer for discover of new local routes in Traefik to essentially run a script as if using `cron` to add `avahi-publish` commands and leave them running to serve the local domain for each. So forking it the right solution, and you helped me discover it quickly when I was stumped for what was happening.

If I rewrite my Bash script in GoLang and allow SystemD to manage the GoLang program then I could have it to publish all five domains and monitor for new domains in the same process. If I do that then I definitely agree that it would be better to let SystemD manage it.  But using `avahi-publish` as I am and given the way it works, I cannot envision how I would do it without the `forking` type.

#fwiw
conversations.answer: I'm glad to hear that changing the service type to forking has resolved your issue!Your thought process on managing your service makes a lot of sense. With the current setup of using a Bash script to add avahi-publish commands, it would indeed be difficult to manage the service without forking, given how avahi-publish works.If you eventually decide to rewrite your script in Go, you could manage the publishing and monitoring in a more integrated way, using the language's capabilities for concurrent processing and network communication. This would indeed allow you to simplify the system-level management by switching back to Type=simple and letting systemd handle it.However, there's certainly nothing wrong with using the forking type when it fits your needs better, as in your current setup. Systemd's flexibility in handling different service types is a strength, and it's there to be used as needed.Best of luck with your project, and don't hesitate to ask if you have any more questions!

conversations.prompt:
I have discovered another issue where the behavior inside the service does not behave the same as if I run in the terminal on the command line.

When I run `pgrep -a avahi-publish` in the terminal on the command line I get the following:
```
1592873 /usr/bin/avahi-publish -a davisworkwear.local -R 192.168.1.110
1592880 /usr/bin/avahi-publish -a dww.local -R 192.168.1.110
1592887 /usr/bin/avahi-publish -a step-ca.local -R 192.168.1.110
1592894 /usr/bin/avahi-publish -a traefik.local -R 192.168.1.110

```

However if I run the same command from within the service and then inspect the logs using sudo `journalctl -u traefik-mdns.service -r` the output is empty.

Are those processes not visible within the service?  And if not, is there any way I can gain access to them?
conversations.answer: It appears you are facing an issue with process visibility when you run your script as a service. When you run the script as a service, it's essentially running in a different environment than when you run it directly from the terminal.The pgrep command is returning empty possibly because the service's environment does not see the avahi-publish processes you started in the terminal. Each service managed by systemd runs in its own process and has its own view of the system.If you want to check if the processes are running from within the service, you could try to use a more explicit form of pgrep that checks all processes, not just the ones owned by the current user:[CODE_BLOCK_0]In the -a option includes the command line in the output, and the -x option matches processes whose names are exactly avahi-publish.If this does not work, you may want to consider a different approach to ensure that the avahi-publish processes are running as expected.You could implement a logging system in your script to log the process IDs of the avahi-publish processes when they are started, then check those logs from within your service.Alternatively, you could run the avahi-publish commands from within your service itself, which should guarantee visibility. You might need to adjust your service to wait for the avahi-publish processes to finish, or to manage them in the background as necessary.

conversations.prompt: After more investigation I am finding that the processes are visible within the service IF they were created outside the service, but if they were created inside the service with an `&` at the end then the service will never see them with `pgrep` or `ps ax`.  Does this help diagnose?
conversations.answer: This is likely related to how bash handles job control, particularly with background jobs, and the interaction with systemd service management.When you append an & to the end of a command in bash, it forks that process to run in the background and continues with the next line of the script immediately. This makes the process a child of the current bash shell, not of the systemd service directly.Systemd services, when they are of the simple or forking type, will only track the main process (the PID it started, or the one that remains after forking). They don't inherently track all child processes. Also, services generally don't implement full job control like an interactive bash shell does.Thus, when your script launches avahi-publish processes into the background, these processes are technically children of the bash process, not of the systemd service. This could be why your service cannot see these processes.There's a few possible solutions here:You could consider using Type=exec in your service file instead of Type=forking. This will allow systemd to track all processes started by the service, not just the main process. However, your service may need to be adjusted to accommodate this.Alternatively, you could use a bash function that tracks the PIDs of the background jobs in a file, and then have your service read this file to check on the status of these processes.Here is an example of such a function:[CODE_BLOCK_0]This function runs the given command in the background and then writes the PID of the process to a file. You can then read this file in your service to get the PIDs of the avahi-publish processes.Remember to clean up the pidfile at the beginning of your script to ensure you're tracking the correct PIDs each time the service runs.

conversations.prompt:
Using `Type=exec` takes us back to the original problem.  
Using  a pid file can easily get out of sync and I'd rather use that as an option of last resort.

Is it not possible to get a list of background processes from within the service?
conversations.answer: Normally, a process running within a service should be able to see other processes in the system, so pgrep or ps ax should work. But your case seems to be a special one because of the way processes are being created and monitored.This problem can arise from a couple of different behaviors:Shell Session Isolation: If you're spawning processes within a shell script, and that shell script is being run by a systemd service, these processes are children of the shell script's process, not the systemd service directly. Therefore, once the shell script completes, these child processes might be getting re-parented to a different process (like init), making them potentially hard to find.PID Namespaces: Systemd services can be run in their own PID namespace, meaning they can only see their own processes, and not any processes on the rest of the system. This is controlled by the PrivateTmp and PrivateNetwork options in the systemd service file. If these are set to true, it could explain why you can't see the avahi-publish processes.Given these complications, it's generally best to structure your systemd service so that it doesn't rely on background processes running in an independent manner. If these are essential, you may want to consider setting up multiple, interdependent systemd services instead.However, if you must do it this way, and don't want to use PID files, you could use the disown command to remove the processes from the shell's job table, which might help make them visible to the service.Here's how you could modify your script:[CODE_BLOCK_0]This will make the processes children of the init process, rather than the shell script, which might make them visible to pgrep. Note that this is a workaround and may not always work as expected.This approach doesn't guarantee that the systemd service will be able to see the processes, but it's an option if you'd rather not use PID files.If you continue to experience issues, I would recommend restructuring your service or application to better work with the way systemd manages processes.

conversations.answer: PrivateTmp and PrivateNetwork are directives you can set in a unit file for a systemd service. They're used to provide the service with its own private /tmp and networking namespace, respectively.To set these directives, you'd open the unit file for your service with a text editor. This file will typically be located in /etc/systemd/system/, and will have a .service extension.In the [Service] section of the file, you can add the following lines to set these directives:[CODE_BLOCK_0]After you've saved and closed the file, you'd run sudo systemctl daemon-reload to make systemd aware of the changes, and then restart your service with sudo systemctl restart your-service.However, please note that setting these options could have unexpected effects, depending on what your service does. For example, if you set PrivateNetwork=true, your service will not be able to make network connections outside of itself, which might not be what you want.The issue you're experiencing with pgrep might not be due to these options being set, but they're worth checking just in case. By default, these options should be set to false, meaning your service should be able to see all processes on the system. If they're set to true, that could explain why you're not seeing the output you expect.As always, you should carefully consider the implications of setting these options before doing so, and test thoroughly to make sure they're not causing other issues with your service.

SystemD service files can be a bit complex, and the environment they provide can sometimes be quite different from a regular shell.If you need to track the processes started by your script, perhaps you could have the script log their PIDs to a file when it starts them, rather than relying on pgrep to find them. You should adjust and elaborate on this solution to fit your exact needs.Remember to ensure that the path where you're storing this PID file (in this case /var/log/my_pids) is writable by the user running the service. If it isn't, you'll need to change the permissions on that path or choose a different path.

avahi-publish -a davisworkwear.local -R 192.168.1.110 & echo $! >> /var/log/my_pids
avahi-publish -a dww.local -R 192.168.1.110 & echo $! >> /var/log/my_pids
avahi-publish -a step-ca.local -R 192.168.1.110 & echo $! >> /var/log/my_pids
avahi-publish -a traefik.local -R 192.168.1.110 & echo $! >> /var/log/my_pids
avahi-publish -a wordpress.local -R 192.168.1.110 & echo $! >> /var/log/my_pids

conversations.prompt:
Well that was plainly a pain. 

I was never able to enable those spawned `avahi-publish` processes to be visible from within the SystemD service, but I was able to find a different approach.

Rather than get a list of available .local domains being published I instead discovered `avahi-resolve` that allowed me to inspect to see if a specific `.local` domain was in-fact already published. The downside of this approach is that if it is not already published then you have to wait for a timeout to determine it has not been publish, but if published it returns quickly/ 

Since this is meant to be a background task running on a timer the timeout will only ever create issues when modifying the script and having to wait for timeout while debugging. Hopefully there won't be much need for that.

conversations.answer: I'm glad you were able to find a solution that works for you, even if it wasn't exactly what you originally envisioned. Your resilience in solving this issue is admirable!Your new approach using avahi-resolve makes sense, given the constraints you were working with. The timeout issue might be a small price to pay, especially if modifications to the script are infrequent.The status output you provided looks good – it seems like your service is running and creating the avahi-publish processes as expected.Systemd can be a complex tool to work with, but it is also very powerful. Your experience here will undoubtedly be helpful in the future when dealing with other services and scripts.If you run into any other issues or have more questions, don't hesitate to ask. Happy coding!
